boot: [0.5 min] Set the stage with the old DOSCloud look from the Atlanta deck. Explain that DOSCloud Mini is a working Node.js application with a browser-based DOSBox-X emulator. Today the application is the demo vehicle; the development environment is the subject.
problem: [1 min] Contrast committing code with committing a repeatable environment. No need to argue that containers solve every problem; the point is to reduce time lost before a developer can make a useful change.
idea: [1 min] Make the distinction between app runtime, container image, and development experience. The dev container definition is a contract for editor setup around a container, not an alternative to Git.
journey: [1 min] The talk is about an hour. Slides give conceptual handles; the demos prove things. Mention that all demo files are committed in the public DOSCloud Mini repository, so the audience can follow along.
mental-model: [1.25 min] Walk left to right. An image provides OS and tools; VS Code or Codespaces manages the workspace, lifecycle and port forwarding. The app is not inherently a dev container.
demo1-intro: [0.25 min] Switch from slides to VS Code. Open the repository root and select the Hello World configuration.
hello-code: [1 min] Point out the absolute minimum: image, optional lifecycle action, and an unprivileged user. The image tag chooses Node 22. No app ports because the example is a CLI hello-world program.
demo1-live: [6 min] Budget six minutes including time for the first container. If a rebuild is slow, use a prebuilt container and jump directly to the output. Ask the audience: what did we put in Git to make this reproducible? Answer: the definition and sample application.
demo1-takeaway: [0.5 min] Keep brief. The initial demo is the baseline for all subsequent additions.
anatomy: [1.25 min] A devcontainer.json is consumed by the Dev Containers tooling (VS Code/Codespaces); do not confuse its `forwardPorts` with Docker's `EXPOSE` or `-p`. Extensions/settings are optional. This talk keeps only the minimum needed by Node.
lifecycle: [1.5 min] Explain `postCreateCommand` runs at creation (not on every terminal), while `postStartCommand` is for each start. The app script checks health before starting to avoid duplicate servers. Rebuild versus reopen is important.
options: [1.25 min] Avoid overengineering: DOSCloud Mini needs Node and npm packages, not Go or a database. Explain when Compose becomes useful for app+database, but the demo remains single service.
demo2-intro: [0.25 min] Open the real repository root and select example 02, then 03. The difference is image acquisition, not the app source or browser UX.
node-config: [1.25 min] The source config also labels the forwarded port. Show why npm ci is more repeatable than an unconstrained install. The server listens on 0.0.0.0:3000 inside the container; its public visibility still depends on forwarding.
dockerfile: [1.25 min] Docker image builds have layered cache semantics. We copy manifests before source and install Node packages into an image path so alternate Docker Compose deployments can resolve dependencies. Avoid extra languages because this application is Node-only.
build-vs-runtime: [1 min] Emphasize changes to the Dockerfile require rebuild; changes to JS often require only restart/watcher. The workspace mount means changing source does not require baking it into each image. Beware the difference between the workspace and ephemeral container storage.
ports: [1 min] Clarify Dockerfile EXPOSE is documentation, VS Code forwardPorts makes the app reachable in development, and docker -p publishes in standalone Docker runs. Codespaces forwards via HTTPS and access control. The emulator needs secure-context APIs, so HTTPS or localhost is important.
demo2-live: [10 min] Allow 10 minutes with ready-to-open containers. The custom image takes time on first build; prebuild it before talk. Verify the browser's address and ensure port 3000 is private. The public repo includes the v1.9 DOOM shareware files. Don't casually upload arbitrary copyrighted games.
gotchas: [1.25 min] Walk through the common failures: app binds to 127.0.0.1 inside container only, wrong forwarded port, invalid image build path, missing npm deps, wrong directory, and browser secure-context restrictions.
cloud-shape: [1.25 min] Codespaces hosts compute/storage remotely; it is not the same local container magically moved. The repo provides definitions; Codespaces creates an independent workspace and forwarded URL. Prebuilds can improve startup if configured, but they are not needed for this demo.
demo3-intro: [0.25 min] Switch to GitHub. The real public repository is https://github.com/theonemule/doscloud-mini .
codespaces-steps: [1 min] A Codespace may choose the root .devcontainer config automatically. Use the config picker for explicit example selection. The production-style DOSCloud app intentionally lacks login, so do not make port 3000 public for an audience demo.
demo3-live: [8 min] Use an existing Codespace as a safety fallback; avoid burning audience time on image pulls. Mention compute cost and sleep behavior briefly, but don't overfocus. Show the actual underlying file paths and the private forwarded port. Browser's secure APIs work on Codespaces HTTPS.
state: [1 min] This bridges to remote development and explains why files you wrote in one Codespace don't materialize on your laptop until committed/pulled. The host C: drive is a persistent workspace directory per instance; guests write into room overlays that are deleted.
remote-shape: [1.25 min] Define each route precisely. Remote-SSH extends the editor to a host, Dev Containers builds the defined environment, Attach-to-Running-Container inspects an existing container. They differ in lifecycle and persistence. Don't suggest attaching automatically gives production parity or safe debugging access.
demo4-intro: [0.25 min] Use the trusted home-lab/dev VM as the remote host; no public exposure needed. If SSH is unreachable from conference Wi-Fi, show the same workflow on a preconnected Remote-SSH window.
remote-vs-attach: [1.25 min] Explain that attachment is not the same as configuring a new dev environment; attached containers may lack an editor server, package manager, or source mount. Use remote host privileges cautiously.
remote-debug: [1.25 min] Run only one server instance: stop the development watcher before starting the inspector. 9229 is *optional*, not in the default devcontainer config, intentionally. Attach from the editor session running on the same remote side or forward it privately. Do not confuse Docker attach, VS Code Attach to Running Container, and Node inspector.
demo4-live: [7 min] Keep a connected VS Code session and prepared breakpoint available. If live debug fails, show the Node inspector console and health endpoint and explain the network path. This demo is more about where development compute runs than about DOS gaming.
dos-persistence: [1 min] This is a natural bridge to source mounts and volume persistence. On room creation, snapshot hardlinks freeze the host base; guest overlay edits are isolated. Do not conflate Git with automatic synchronization or promise block-level COW.
guardrails: [1 min] Remind audience that Codespaces port visibility is distinct from having a URL. The app is a controlled demonstration. Keeping the public source readable and the data scope intentional is part of a good conference demo.
final: [0.75 min] Recap the concept rather than every command. A dev container moves from environment setup tribal knowledge to a versioned contract.
resources: [0.5 min] Leave this visible long enough for photos and note-taking. All three Node-only examples are in the same repo; the root default is equivalent to example 03.
qa: [1.5 min] If time is tight, cut before Q&A; if ahead, invite questions about network forwarding, Codespaces privacy, Docker layers, or debugger port safety.
